turns.prompt_text: Is there such thing as existential positivity
turns.response_html:
Absolutely. In fact, it is a well-established branch of philosophy and psychology.

When people hear "existentialism," they usually think of existential dread—the heavy, angsty feeling that life has no inherent meaning, the universe is indifferent, and we are completely on our own.

But existential positivity (often explored through optimistic nihilism, existential humanism, or the works of thinkers like Albert Camus and Viktor Frankl) looks at that exact same blank slate and sees it as the ultimate form of freedom.

If the universe doesn't hand you a pre-written script, it means you have total agency to write your own.

Here is how the positive side of existentialism breaks down, and why it is actually incredibly liberating:

1. Radical Freedom (Jean-Paul Sartre)

Sartre famously wrote that humans are "condemned to be free." While that sounds ominous, the flip side is pure positivity. If there is no grand cosmic blueprint or destiny dictating who you have to be, you are entirely responsible for defining yourself.

  • The Positive Shift: You aren't stuck dealing with a pre-determined fate. Every choice you make is an act of self-creation. You get to decide what your values are, what kind of person you want to be, and how you want to interact with the world.

2. The Absurd Hero (Albert Camus)

Camus looked at the "Absurd"—the conflict between humans desperately searching for meaning and a cold, silent universe that refuses to give them one. Instead of giving in to despair, Camus suggested we should rebel by living defiantly, passionately, and happily anyway.

  • The Positive Shift: In his essay The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus imagines the mythological man condemned to push a boulder up a hill for eternity, only to watch it roll back down every time. Camus concludes that "one must imagine Sisyphus happy." The joy is found in the conscious act of pushing, the effort itself, and the refusal to let the meaninglessness of the task crush your spirit.

3. Optimistic Nihilism

This is a modern, secular take on existential positivity. Nihilism says nothing matters on a cosmic scale. Optimistic nihilism looks at that and says, "Great! That means all your mistakes, embarrassments, and failures don't matter to the cosmos either."

  • The Positive Shift: It removes immense pressure. If the universe doesn't care, you are free to enjoy the life you have right now. It reframes our brief existence not as a test we might fail, but as a rare, miraculous window of time where we get to experience consciousness, taste good food, run, build things, and appreciate the world.

4. Tragic Optimism (Viktor Frankl)

Frankl, a neurologist, psychiatrist, and Holocaust survivor, developed a framework called Logotherapy based on his experiences. He argued that the primary human drive isn't pleasure or power, but the search for meaning. He coined the term "tragic optimism," which is the capacity to remain optimistic even in the face of pain, guilt, and death.

  • The Positive Shift: Frankl argued that meaning isn't something you find lying around; it's something you construct out of three things:
    1. By creating a work or doing a deed. (Building, creating, working on a project).
    2. By experiencing something or encountering someone. (Love, nature, art).
    3. By the attitude we take toward unavoidable suffering.

The Core Takeaway: Existential positivity doesn't ask you to ignore the chaotic, messy, or indifferent parts of reality. Instead, it tells you that because the world is a blank canvas, you are the author of your own meaning. You don't have to discover a hidden purpose; you get to choose what matters to you and dedicate your energy to it.

Does a specific aspect of this—like the idea of radical freedom versus cosmic pressure—rest resonate more with what you're thinking about?
